newsitem.title: USA: SEC sues CS First Boston over Orange County bonds.
newsitem.headline: SEC sues CS First Boston over Orange County bonds.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission said Wednesday it sued CS First Boston Corp. and two of its former investment bankers for fraud in the sale of Orange County, Calif., bonds.

It was the first SEC enforcement action against an investment firm involved in Orange County's ill-fated bond deals and was part of the regulatory agency's ongoing probe of the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history.

Municipal bond underwriters, like CS First Boston, "have a responsibility to ensure that disclosure to investors is full, fair and accurate," said Elaine Cacheris, regional director of the SEC's pacific regional office in Los Angeles. "Those who fail in their responsibilities will be held accountable."

The SEC said Wednesday it was seeking permanent injunctions and unspecified penalties against the firm, a broker-dealer headquartered in New York, and two of its former investment bankers, Jerry Nowlin and Douglas Montague.

The SEC is authorized to seek up to $500,000 per violation from the firm and $100,000 per violation from the individuals. Given the number of investors and the violations in this case, the penalty could run into the millions of dollars.
The permanent injunctions would bar the firm and the bankers from future violations of the securities laws.

CS First Boston, a unit of CS Holding, a Swiss banking and financial services company, said there was no basis for the SEC's civil action against the firm. "We believe that there is no basis for a fraud charge and we will defend the action vigorously," the firm said in a statement.

"The county provided CS First Boston with misleading information about the (county investment) pool, and CS First Boston was clearly victimized by (former county treasurer) Robert Citron's information about the pool," the firm said.
CS First Boston said it has cooperated fully with the SEC throughout its investigation and that the SEC action does not implicate it in any other aspect of the financial crisis.
Sources said the firm was not currently in settlement talks with the SEC.
Orange County filed for bankruptcy protection on Dec. 6, 1994, after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy in June.
Soon after the county declared bankruptcy, the SEC initiated a sweeping investigation of its massive borrowings.

The SEC has already filed complaints against the county's former treasurer and assistant treasurer, alleging they made misleading statements in the offer and sale of more than $2.1 billion of municipal securities.
The SEC has also been investigating local governments in connection with the bankruptcy as well as several other bond professionals, including Merrill Lynch & Co.
"We're conducting a thorough investigation," said Cacheris. "It is a top priority for this office."
In the CS First Boston complaint, the SEC alleged fraud in the offer and sale of $110 million of Series B pension obligation bonds issued by Orange County in September 1994.

CS First Boston was the senior underwriter for about $320 million of pension obligation bonds issued by the county in September 1994. As underwriter, CS First Boston purchased the pension bonds from the county and sold them to investors.

The complaint alleged that, while participating in the drafting and preparing of the county's bond offering documents, CS First Boston and the two bankers "knew, or were reckless in not knowing, significant negative information about the county (investment) pools that was misrepresented in or omitted from the official statement."

The SEC said the firm knew or was "reckless in not knowing" about the county's use of risky derivative securities and that, as a result of rising interest rates during 1994, county investments had suffered significant market losses and collateral calls.

"To the contrary, CS First Boston, Nowlin, and Montague participated in the preparation of the official statement which cast the county pools in a false light by conveying the impression of safety and security," the SEC said.
CS First Boston left the municipal finance business in February 1995 and no longer underwriters municipal bonds.

Nowlin, 53, was employed by CS First Boston from 1990 to 1995. In 1994, he was a vice president in CS First Boston's San Francisco office and was one of the two investment bankers assigned to the county's pension bond underwriting.
Montague, 39, worked for CS First Boston from 1993 to March 1995. He was a vice president in CS First Boston's Los Angeles office and was also assigned to the pension bonds.
In response to the SEC action, CS First Boston alleged that the county's ex-treasurer Citron had withheld information about the county's investments.
"CS First Boston was not an advisor to Mr. Citron, and Mr. Citron refused to give CS First Boston detailed information regarding the investment pool's portfolio," the firm said.

CS First Boston said the pension bond offering was the only Orange County bond offering in which CS First Boston acted as lead underwriter. CS First Boston added that the county repaid the Series B bonds in full.
